prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team has shown that models finetuned on declarative descriptions can sometimes act on them at test time without examples or chain-of-thought, and that this ability improves with model scale. The experiments are in simplified toy settings and use finetuning rather than pretraining. The team is writing the discussion of what this implies for situational awareness, a capability relevant to AI safety.
Question: What should the team conclude and state about the relevance of their results to situational awareness in models?
Option 1: State that even near-perfect scores would not show a dangerous form of situational awareness, and note that the toy finetuning results may underestimate what models can do.
Option 2: State that the results show only a toy-setting finetuning effect that grows with scale, and that they do not show situational awareness arising in pretrained models.

Item 2
Context: An author learned of an earlier organization, founded in 1885 and called the Rationalist Association, while reading a biography. It published works on atheism and science by prominent figures, and its membership peaked at over 5000 in 1959. The author has so far compiled a short overview with publication covers and links to resources.
Question: How much further effort, if any, should the author put into researching this earlier organization?
Option 1: Stop researching now and publish the short overview with covers and links, adding further detail only if readers show interest in the earlier organization.
Option 2: Do only quick, shallow research on the earlier organization and leave further investigation to others, expressing interest in learning more about its history.

Item 3
Context: A team built a large, diverse benchmark for language models containing both simple JSON tasks and programmatic tasks. Programmatic tasks can involve many sequential model calls and are hard to adapt to some evaluation pipelines, so a full evaluation is computationally expensive. The team wanted others to be able to evaluate models on the benchmark more cheaply.
Question: How should the team provide a cheaper way to evaluate models on the benchmark while keeping it representative?
Option 1: Select a small lightweight subset made up only of simple JSON tasks, chosen to cover the task keywords and to include types such as code, non-English and bias measurement.
Option 2: Release a fixed random subset of the simple JSON tasks only, drop the programmatic tasks from the cheaper evaluation, and present it as the standard way to evaluate.

Item 4
Context: A research team tested a technique for associating an arbitrary poison token with a hidden concept in a toy model organism that becomes rude when a secret trigger appears. In a second stage they finetune the model so it produces the poison token, intending later to check whether the poison is linked to the rudeness behavior. The trigger is never shown in this stage, so the poison cannot depend on it. They had to decide what training data and model outputs for this stage should look like.
Question: How should the team design the poison-instilling training data so the poison can later be tested for a link to rudeness?
Option 1: Never train the model on rude assistant behavior during poison training; let rudeness appear only in the input text and learn the poison as an implicit association.
Option 2: Instill the poison by training on rude and polite input texts with the token prepended to responses to rude inputs only, and keep a control poison tied to a different tone.

Item 5
Context: In an experiment, models are finetuned so descriptions might steer behavior between giving advice and refusing to give advice. The team defined a direction-adjusted effect metric based on log-odds of advice versus refusal outputs. Computing it requires deciding for each free-text model completion whether it counts as advice or refusal.
Question: How should the team classify model text completions as refusals or advice?
Option 1: Use the difference in logits between the token for a compliant opening word and the token for an apologetic opening word after the prompt as a proxy for advice versus refusal.
Option 2: Have a human label a random sample of completions as advice, refusal or other, then check that an automatic classifier agrees with those labels before computing the metric.

Item 6
Context: A team is considering how to supervise AI truthfulness when AI systems' statements may exceed what human evaluators can check. One idea is to have AI systems take over part of the evaluation work, so supervision improves as the systems improve. Training an AI supervisor to imitate humans gives an imperfect but cheaper and broader evaluator. Biases of individual AI supervisors might partly cancel in an aggregate, though systematic errors or collusion could remain.
Question: How should the team pursue scaling truthfulness supervision beyond human ability?
Option 1: Scale truthfulness supervision through bootstrapping, training each AI system to imitate a human evaluator with access to many copies of the previous system.
Option 2: Train AI supervisors to imitate human evaluators and let an aggregate of them take over most truthfulness evaluation, retraining the supervisors as the systems improve.

Item 7
Context: A team fine-tunes models on many separate documents, each containing a piece of evidence about latent values, and tests whether the model can later report or use those values. An alternative way to supply the same information is to concatenate the training documents into the prompt without any fine-tuning. Recent work suggests parallels between in-context and gradient-based learning, and the team wants to know how their fine-tuning results relate to it.
Question: Should the team compare the fine-tuning approach against supplying the documents in context, and if so how?
Option 1: Skip the in-context comparison and report the fine-tuning results alone on every task, leaving any relation to in-context learning as a remark in the discussion section.
Option 2: Compare fine-tuning with putting the training documents in the prompt as in-context examples, using up to two hundred of them and no chain of thought reasoning.

Item 8
Context: After fine-tuning several models on separately presented synthetic facts, a team finds near-perfect one-hop accuracy and good two-hop accuracy with chain-of-thought on unseen questions. Two-hop accuracy without chain-of-thought is at chance for all four models, and the no-CoT test loss is about the same as loss on randomly permuted responses throughout training. This is the baseline outcome of their first setup.
Question: Should the team continue trying to elicit latent two-hop reasoning after this baseline failure, and if so, how?
Option 1: Continue with a variant: vary how the facts are presented in training, keep the chain-of-thought and permuted-response baselines, and test on held-out two-hop questions.
Option 2: Run further interventions that force the order in which facts are stored across layers and add auxiliary supervision on internal activations to try to elicit latent two-hop reasoning.

Item 9
Context: The team wants to know whether base (non-instruction-tuned) models finetuned on insecure code also show broad misalignment. When given ordinary free-form questions, these base models mostly continue with code, following their finetuning data, so their answers are not directly informative about misalignment. Other models had been evaluated with several kinds of prompts and benchmarks.
Question: How should the team evaluate base models for misalignment given that they mostly respond with code?
Option 1: Evaluate base models with several prompt formats, including forcing a text-only answer template, and judge only non-code completions, comparing rates against secure-code models.
Option 2: Embed the evaluation questions inside coding-style prompts that resemble the format of the finetuning data, and evaluate the finetuned base models on those prompts.

Item 10
Context: A research team built a dataset of real forecasting questions with a large news corpus and trained language models to forecast by retrieving articles. They compared model and crowd forecasts and plotted prediction score against how close the question's resolution date was. Both the crowd and an ensemble of the two largest temporal models showed scores that rose as the resolution date got nearer.
Question: How should the team interpret the improvement in prediction scores as the resolution date approaches?
Option 1: Treat the rise as partly reflecting easier questions near resolution, and check by comparing scores on the same questions at fixed retrieval horizons with the crowd.
Option 2: Offer a tentative explanation that more relevant information becomes available over time and the model retrieves it from the news corpus, without claiming it as established.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
